papers.title: On human-in-the-loop optimization of human–robot interaction
papers.authors_short: Slade, Atkeson, Donelan, Houdijk, Ingraham, Kim, Kong, Poggensee, Riener, Steinert, Zhang, Collins
papers.api_title: On human-in-the-loop optimization of human–robot interaction
papers.core_idea: Perspective by twelve HILO groups: because human responses to devices cannot be modelled or predicted accurately enough, empirically optimize device characteristics on each user's measured performance; it walks through each key HILO decision across contexts and lists open algorithmic and scientific questions.
papers.what_to_take: Use its walkthrough of key HILO decisions as the checklist for the later human-study plan, and to state which of those decisions SMAT-style simulation replaces or merely assumes.
papers.left_untested: Perspective without new data. Full text was paywalled and not read here, so whether it treats sprinting or models adaptation-optimizer interaction quantitatively is unchecked; read it before citing specifics.
papers.feasibility_notes: Reading only; nature.com redirected to a login page on 2026-09-23, so institutional access is needed.

papers.title: How adaptation, training, and customization contribute to benefits from exoskeleton assistance
papers.code_status: none known; paywalled full text not inspected (status as of 2026-09-23)
papers.api_title: How adaptation, training, and customization contribute to benefits from exoskeleton assistance
papers.core_idea: Naïve users learned ankle-exoskeleton walking under low-, moderate- or high-variation training. After moderate-variation training, customized assistance cut metabolic rate 39% versus exo off; training supplied about half, customization a quarter. Expertise took about 109 min; optimal peak torque kept rising.
papers.what_to_take: Calibration targets for any claim that simulated stages mirror acclimation: hours-scale expertise, training-type effects, users drawing less exoskeleton power as expertise grows, and slower drift in optimal torque magnitude than other parameters.
papers.left_untested: Ankle only, treadmill walking, metabolic objective; no hip, running or sprint conditions. The abstract reports descriptive time courses, not a predictive adaptation model a simulation could be fitted to.
papers.feasibility_notes: Reading only; use its reported timescales as priors when mapping simulated stages onto human sessions.

papers.title: Human adaptation to adaptive machines converges to game-theoretic equilibria
papers.code_status: official: data and analysis scripts stated to be in Code Ocean capsule 6746258 (returned HTTP 403 to script); experiment web code at github.com/dynams/web, no licence, last push 2026-07-04 (checked 2026-09-23)
papers.api_title: Human adaptation to adaptive machines converges to game-theoretic equilibria
papers.core_idea: Crowd-sourced participants co-adapted with machines in two-player games with prescribed quadratic costs. With machine gradient descent, outcomes shifted from Nash (slowest machine rate) to human-led Stackelberg (fastest); policy-space algorithms steered play, even to the machine's optimum, without inverse-estimating human cost.
papers.what_to_take: Device update rate selects the equilibrium when the human best-responds. Rate changes alone leave simultaneous-gradient stationary points unchanged, so attribute SMAT stage effects to freezing or basin selection, not human-like timing.
papers.left_untested: Low-dimensional manual-input games on a screen with prescribed costs; no physical assistance, musculoskeletal dynamics, fatigue or locomotion. Whether wearers best-respond to exoskeleton updates this way is untested.
papers.feasibility_notes: A toy quadratic game with a simulated best-responding human tests the Nash/Stackelberg shift on CPU in minutes.

papers.title: Exo-Plore: Exploring Exoskeleton Control Space through Human-aligned Simulation
papers.code_status: official, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; C++/Python, PPO via Ray RLlib; ~20 GB experiment data on OneDrive; last push 2026-08-04 (checked 2026-09-23)
papers.api_title: Exo-Plore: Exploring Exoskeleton Control Space through Human-aligned Simulation
papers.core_idea: A neuromechanical deep-RL human, rewarded for metabolic minimization plus a human-exoskeleton-interaction term chosen to match experimental adaptation trends, generates assisted gaits across sampled hip-assistance settings; a neural cost-of-transport surrogate then gives gradient-optimized gain and delay per speed without human trials.
papers.what_to_take: The closest occupied claim to simulated co-adaptation: here 'adaptation' is an RL human's adapted steady state per setting. Reuse its surrogate-plus-gradient optimizer and its checks against published assisted-gait trends.
papers.left_untested: No human validation of the optimized settings (authors' stated limitation); adaptation dynamics and timescales are not modelled; walking only. Authors flag stateless Hill muscles as particularly problematic for fast running.
papers.feasibility_notes: Code public but non-commercial; RL gait generator plus C++ rollouts suit the 64-core EPYC; the paper's surrogate experiments used an RTX 3070.

papers.title: Simulating human-in-the-loop optimization of exoskeleton assistance to compare optimization algorithm performance
papers.venue: bioRxiv preprint (v1 2024-04-09; no journal version listed by bioRxiv)
papers.code_status: official, MIT; Jupyter notebooks, dataset spreadsheet and saved GP models; last push 2024-04-11; the paper's Harvard-Ability-Lab link redirects here (checked 2026-09-23)
papers.api_title: Simulating human-in-the-loop optimization of exoskeleton assistance to compare optimization algorithm performance
papers.core_idea: Gaussian-process surrogates of the metabolic landscape, fitted to five subjects' CMA-ES ankle-exoskeleton HILO data, replace measurements to simulate HILO for experts (static landscape), novices (landscape interpolated between subjects over 80 evaluations, ~160 min) and 4-20 parameters, comparing CMA-ES, cross-entropy, BO and exploitative BO.
papers.what_to_take: A cheap, reusable bench for optimizer and update-schedule comparisons: BO variants converged fastest for static experts (~60 evaluations), exploitative BO tracked the drifting novice optimum best, and no algorithm won everywhere.
papers.left_untested: Adaptation is linear interpolation between two subjects' landscapes, not a learning process; surrogates were fitted to non-uniform CMA-ES samples; ankle walking only; simulated rankings were not tested prospectively in people.
papers.feasibility_notes: local PDF; notebooks are CPU-light; swap in a sprint-time surrogate from the musculoskeletal sprinter.

papers.title: Validation of Dynamic Bayesian Optimization for Human-in-the-Loop Optimization of Exoskeleton Control at User-Driven Walking Speed
papers.code_status: no code or data link in the bioRxiv v1 PDF (checked 2026-09-23)
papers.api_title: Validation of Dynamic Bayesian Optimization for Human-in-the-Loop Optimization of Exoskeleton Control at User-Driven Walking Speed
papers.core_idea: Sixteen adults completed two counterbalanced 40-iteration HILO visits with a bilateral hip exoskeleton (torque-pulse amplitude, timing, duration) maximizing speed on a user-driven treadmill. Dynamic BO, whose time kernel down-weights older observations, exceeded BO's speed gains at three of four validation iterations.
papers.what_to_take: Treat the wearer as non-stationary: time-decaying kernels, interleaved validation iterations, counterbalanced optimizer order and a variability-matched sham form the design pattern for any later human comparison of update schedules.
papers.left_untested: Walking capped at 1.6 m/s, 40 iterations per visit, healthy adults, sham tested in only three participants; no running or sprinting, and no learning model separating adaptation from fatigue or noise.
papers.feasibility_notes: local PDF; DBO is a small change to any GP-BO library and can be tested first on the Kutulakos bench.

papers.title: Human Machine Co-Adaptation Model and Its Convergence Analysis
papers.code_status: none cited in the arXiv v1 PDF (KB copy searched 2026-09-23)
papers.api_title: Human Machine Co-Adaptation Model and Its Convergence Analysis
papers.core_idea: Cooperative adaptive MDP of patient and robot with factored private and shared states: sufficient conditions for alternating policy iteration to converge and for a unique Nash equilibrium, epsilon-greedy updates to escape local equilibria, and a threshold-update loss bound, all on random finite MDPs.
papers.what_to_take: Baselines, not guarantees: fixed alternation, threshold-gated updates, restricted human policy sets and robot-side exploration are comparison arms for SMAT schedules; the KB digest lists printed inconsistencies to resolve first.
papers.left_untested: Exact tabular policy iteration, ergodic continuing chains and an information condition; no neural policies, simultaneous learning, episodic sprint objectives, participants or hardware (KB reading-06).
papers.feasibility_notes: CPU-scale: small random CaMDPs reproduce the theory; use them as a sanity test before PPO-scale schedule runs.

papers.title: Human Machine Co-adaption Interface via Cooperation Markov Decision Process System
papers.authors_short: Guo, Cheng, Li, Li, Duffield, Su
papers.venue: arXiv preprint; final article Knowledge-Based Systems 291:111572 (2024), doi 10.1016/j.knosys.2024.111572 (content equivalence not established)
papers.code_status: none cited in the arXiv v1 PDF (KB copy searched 2026-09-23)
papers.api_title: Human Machine Co-adaption Interface via Cooperation Markov Decision Process System
papers.core_idea: Treats robot-assisted rehabilitation as cooperative multi-agent RL between patient and robot (co-adaptive MDPs) and proposes policy-improvement rules, alternation and instantaneous or accumulated value-improvement thresholds, to curb non-stationarity from mutual learning; validated only by a numerical example.
papers.what_to_take: Source of the accumulated-threshold rule and the eta/(1-gamma) loss bound for a fixed partner; include threshold-gated device updates as a matched-budget arm in schedule comparisons.
papers.left_untested: Finite high-level states and actions, no fitted wearer model or measured adaptation rate, no physical experiment; window M, reset and stopping semantics are ambiguous (KB reading-05).
papers.feasibility_notes: The 2024 journal version is closed access and unread; the arXiv precursor is in the KB.

papers.title: Human-in-the-loop optimization of exoskeleton assistance during walking
papers.authors_short: Zhang, Fiers, Witte, Jackson, Poggensee, Atkeson, Collins
papers.code_status: none known; paywalled full text not inspected (status as of 2026-09-23)
papers.api_title: Human-in-the-loop optimization of exoskeleton assistance during walking
papers.core_idea: Landmark exoskeleton HILO: CMA-ES tuned ankle torque-profile parameters from rapid metabolic estimates during walking. Optimized one-ankle assistance cut metabolic energy 24.2 ± 7.4% versus zero torque; the approach also worked bilaterally, across conditions, during running and for muscle-activity objectives.
papers.what_to_take: Reference protocol and effect sizes for later human work; its finding that a good generic pattern, customization and user learning all contributed is the empirical basis for separating those factors in simulation claims.
papers.left_untested: Tethered ankle emulator, treadmill, metabolic objective with minutes per evaluation; no hip assistance or sprinting, and user learning during optimization was not modelled.
papers.feasibility_notes: Reading only (paywalled); metabolic HILO protocols do not transfer to maximal sprint trials.

papers.title: Human-in-the-loop optimization of hip assistance with a soft exosuit during walking
papers.code_status: none known; paywalled full text not inspected (status as of 2026-09-23)
papers.api_title: Human-in-the-loop optimization of hip assistance with a soft exosuit during walking
papers.core_idea: Bayesian optimization of the peak and offset timing of hip-extension assistance from a textile exosuit found optima in 21.4 ± 1.0 min and cut walking metabolic cost 17.4 ± 3.2% versus no device, revealing participant-specific metabolic landscapes.
papers.what_to_take: Closest hip precedent: two timing parameters, BO under noisy metabolic signals, and evidence that optimal hip timing is individual; its timing parameterization is a comparator for learned sprint assistance.
papers.left_untested: Treadmill walking, hip extension only, metabolic objective; no running, sprinting or flexion assistance, and BO assumed the user's response was stationary.
papers.feasibility_notes: Reading only (paywalled); a two-parameter timing landscape is easy to emulate as a simulated-HILO test case.

papers.title: Humans Can Continuously Optimize Energetic Cost during Walking
papers.code_status: none known; paywalled full text not inspected (status as of 2026-09-23)
papers.api_title: Humans Can Continuously Optimize Energetic Cost during Walking
papers.core_idea: Exoskeletons shifted walkers' energetically optimal step frequency; people converged on the new optimum within minutes, for savings under 5%, and after perturbations re-converged within seconds using an updated prediction, showing continuous real-time optimization of energetic cost.
papers.what_to_take: The human partner is itself a fast, noisy energy optimizer; frozen or slowly updated simulated humans misrepresent this, so report which human timescale, if any, each SMAT stage stands for.
papers.left_untested: One gait parameter (step frequency) in walking under imposed cost gradients; not whether multi-joint sprint coordination adapts on similar timescales, or how people respond to a controller that itself adapts.
papers.feasibility_notes: Reading only; its timescales (minutes to converge, seconds to re-converge) are candidate priors for a rate-limited simulated human.

papers.title: Using dynamic Bayesian optimization to induce desired effects in the presence of motor learning: a simulation study
papers.venue: Computer Methods in Biomechanics and Biomedical Engineering, online 2025-12-03 (bioRxiv 10.1101/2024.08.13.607783)
papers.code_status: no code or data link in the bioRxiv v2 full text; journal version paywalled (checked 2026-09-23)
papers.api_title: Using dynamic Bayesian optimization to induce desired effects in the presence of motor learning: a simulation study
papers.core_idea: Simulated HILO in which participant responses follow purely time-dependent drift or state-space motor-learning models (error-based adaptation plus use-dependent learning). Dynamic BO, adding time to the kernel, was never inferior to BO and overtook it once enough iterations separated learning from noise.
papers.what_to_take: Template for putting an explicit, parameterized human-learning model in the loop, so device-update schedules are compared against known adaptation rates rather than an uncalibrated learning agent.
papers.left_untested: Low-dimensional input-output responses, not musculoskeletal locomotion; the state-space learners are generic motor-learning models, not fitted to exoskeleton wearers; no deep-RL device policies or sprint objectives.
papers.feasibility_notes: Minutes on CPU; couple its state-space learner to a sprint-time surrogate to screen schedules before GPU runs.

papers.title: Metabolic cost adaptations during training with a soft exosuit assisting the hip joint
papers.authors_short: Panizzolo, Freisinger, Karavas, Eckert-Erdheim, Siviy, Long, Zifchock, LaFiandra, Walsh
papers.code_status: none (no code or data statement found in the PMC full text) (checked 2026-09-23)
papers.api_title: Metabolic cost adaptations during training with a soft exosuit assisting the hip joint
papers.core_idea: Over five sessions in 20 days of loaded walking (20.4 kg) with a hip-assisting soft exosuit, metabolic benefit versus unpowered grew from -6.2% to -10.3%, plateaued by session three (about two 20-minute sessions) and was retained five months later.
papers.what_to_take: Hip-specific adaptation timescale for planning human sessions: benefits grow over the first sessions, so familiarize participants before measuring any simulation-derived controller, and report session number.
papers.left_untested: Fixed controller, loaded treadmill walking, metabolic outcome; no optimization during adaptation and no running or sprinting.
papers.feasibility_notes: Reading only (open access); treat its session-level timescale as a prior, not a model.

papers.title: Optimizing Exoskeleton Assistance for Faster Self-Selected Walking
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering 29:786-795
papers.code_status: unknown; PMC full text not retrievable by script (status as of 2026-09-23)
papers.api_title: Optimizing Exoskeleton Assistance for Faster Self-Selected Walking
papers.core_idea: HILO of ankle-exoskeleton torque for self-selected speed on a self-paced treadmill: speed-optimized assistance made ten participants walk 42% faster than in normal shoes and faster than energy-optimized torque, with highly variable gaits and cost-of-transport changes from -31% to +78%.
papers.what_to_take: A speed or time objective yields different, highly individual optima than energy objectives; do not assume SMAT's muscle-activation outcome predicts sprint-time-optimal assistance.
papers.left_untested: Walking only, tethered ankle exoskeletons; no running, sprinting or hip assistance, and no account of how user adaptation shaped the optimizer's speed estimates.
papers.feasibility_notes: Reading only; its self-paced speed objective is the protocol analogue of simulated time-to-distance objectives.

papers.title: Improving the energy economy of human running with powered and unpowered ankle exoskeleton assistance
papers.code_status: none known; paywalled full text not inspected (status as of 2026-09-23)
papers.api_title: Improving the energy economy of human running with powered and unpowered ankle exoskeleton assistance
papers.core_idea: HILO of powered and spring-like ankle-exoskeleton torque during treadmill running: optimized powered assistance improved energy economy 24.7% versus zero torque and 14.6% versus normal shoes, while spring-like assistance was ineffective; optima varied but shared high positive work and late peak timing.
papers.what_to_take: The only running HILO found: powered, positive-work assistance helped where spring-like assistance did not, supporting positive-power targets for sprint assistance; its 'up to 10% faster' is an extrapolation, not a measurement.
papers.left_untested: Steady treadmill running, ankle only, metabolic objective with long evaluations; no sprinting, acceleration, hip assistance or measured speed gain, and adaptation during optimization was not modelled.
papers.feasibility_notes: Reading only (paywalled); metabolic running HILO is not transferable to maximal sprint trials.

papers.title: A Dual Control Approach to Solve Exploration Versus Exploitation Trade-Offs in the Design of Personalized Physical Exercise Sessions
papers.api_title: A Dual Control Approach to Solve Exploration Versus Exploitation Trade-Offs in the Design of Personalized Physical Exercise Sessions
papers.core_idea: Casts personalized exercise-session design as dual control: inputs trade immediate exercise effect against Fisher-information parameter learning weighted by control relevance. In a simulated muscle-compartment (Kegel) model, more information weight cut estimation error but also reduced same-session exercise effect.
papers.what_to_take: Probing versus exploiting is already formalized; any 'informative assistance' or exploration-bonus claim for the device needs a dual-control comparator and must count probing cost (KB reading-07).
papers.left_untested: Simulation only, batch design between sessions; no wearable robot, locomotion or participants; printed recurrences and sensitivity equations need clarification before reimplementation (KB reading-07).
papers.feasibility_notes: CPU-scale; the KB digest documents the equation issues; build an independent dual-control baseline only if an exploration claim is made.

cluster_lessons: Real adaptation is slow and multi-timescale: novice ankle-exoskeleton users needed about 109 min of assisted walking to become expert while their optimal torque magnitude kept drifting (Poggensee & Collins 2021); hip-exosuit benefit plateaued after about two 20-min sessions and persisted five months (Panizzolo 2019); step frequency re-optimizes within minutes and re-converges within seconds (Selinger 2015). SMAT stages have no calibrated mapping onto these times, so report stage length in environment steps and do not call stages human acclimation phases without a calibration.

Two gradient learners are not a wearer and a device. With a best-responding human, the machine's adaptation rate moved outcomes from Nash to human-led Stackelberg, and the authors note that rate changes alone do not move the stationary points of simultaneous gradient play (Chasnov et al. 2025). In SMAT it is freezing one actor that creates leader-follower structure; report learning-rate or stage-length effects as optimisation-dynamics effects and use cross-play between checkpoints to test which equilibrium was reached.

Co-adaptation convergence results (Guo 2023 / KBS 2024; Su 2025) need finite MDPs, exact alternating policy iteration, ergodic chains and an information condition. None holds for PPO musculoskeletal sprint episodes with absorbing finish states, so use them to define baselines (fixed alternation, instantaneous and accumulated thresholds) and a tabular sanity test, never as a guarantee (KB readings 05-06).

Non-stationary partners break standard optimisers: time-varying landscapes slowed BO and favoured exploitative or forgetting variants in simulation (Kutulakos & Slade 2024; Kim, Chishty & Sergi 2025), and a time-decaying kernel beat standard BO in hip-exoskeleton speed HILO (Kim & Sergi 2026). Any update-schedule comparison should include a device-side forgetting baseline and a novice-drift scenario.

The objective changes the optimum: speed-optimal ankle assistance differed from energy-optimal assistance and was idiosyncratic (Song & Collins 2021). SMAT's reported outcomes are walking muscle activation and metabolic cost; sprint-time-optimal assistance has to be optimised and reported on its own terms, not inferred from walking-optimal timing.

Simulated HILO is established practice, with surrogate landscapes (Kutulakos & Slade 2024), explicit motor-learning models (Kim, Chishty & Sergi 2025) and an RL neuromechanical human (Exo-Plore 2026). Each models a fixed landscape, a low-dimensional learner or an adapted steady state; none reproduces a wearer's multi-joint learning trajectory. Exo-Plore also flags stateless Hill muscles as problematic for fast running, a validity caveat for sprint simulation.

No HILO of sprint assistance was found (searches on 2026-09-23). Running HILO is ankle, treadmill and metabolic (Witte 2020), and the sprint exosuit copied a simulation-derived hip profile under admittance control, leaving individual optimisation to future work (Moon et al. 2023, local PDF scirobotics.adf5611.pdf). Fatigue will limit later human sprint work to a few evaluations, which favours simulation-seeded priors and few-shot or preference-based tuning. That work stays human-run and lab-gated.

In people, device updates and training exposure are confounded: biofeedback doubled energy savings and reached fully-adapted-level benefit in a quarter of the time (Lakmazaheri & Collins 2026), and an adaptive-gain controller shortened adaptation to about a third (Koller et al. 2015). Human comparisons of update schedules therefore need exposure-matched, counterbalanced, sham-controlled designs like Kim & Sergi 2026.
occupied_claims: Optimising hip-exoskeleton gain and delay in simulation alone, with an RL neuromechanical human that adapts across assistance settings: Exo-Plore (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2601.22550).

Simulating HILO on fitted surrogate landscapes to choose optimisers, including a novice-adaptation scenario: Kutulakos & Slade 2024 (bioRxiv). Hip-exoskeleton surrogate version: Mohammadzadeh Gonabadi et al., Front. Robot. AI 2025 (doi 10.3389/frobt.2025.1669600). EMG-surrogate version: Gonabadi et al., J. Sens. Actuator Netw. 2025 (doi 10.3390/jsan14060113). Online simulated metabolic cost inside real hip-exoskeleton HILO: Gordon et al., IEEE T-RO 2022 (doi 10.1109/TRO.2021.3133137).
Time-aware (dynamic) Bayesian optimisation for non-stationary human responses, in simulation and in hip-exoskeleton walking-speed HILO: Kim, Chishty & Sergi 2025; Kim & Sergi 2026.

Alternating or threshold-gated policy updates for human-machine co-adaptation, with convergence conditions: Guo et al. (arXiv 2023; KBS 2024) and Su et al. 2025. The same group extended this to dual-agent RL co-adaptation: Li, Han, Liu & Su, arXiv 2603.06163 (2026).

The machine's adaptation rate or policy selects the equilibrium human-machine co-adaptation reaches: Chasnov et al. 2025. Related claims: an algorithm reaching the human's cost minimum from observed actions (Isa, Ratliff & Burden, arXiv 2501.08626, 2025); mid-range machine learning rates as the sweet spot for two co-adapting learners (Müller et al., J. Neural Eng. 2017, doi 10.1088/1741-2552/aa620b); differential-game pHRI control (Li et al., Nat. Mach. Intell. 2019, doi 10.1038/s42256-018-0010-3).

Joint multi-agent RL of a musculoskeletal human and a hip exoskeleton in simulation: SMAT (arXiv 2603.07618, 2608.00715), UniExo (arXiv 2609.19690, includes running), and Sun et al., Med. Biol. Eng. Comput. 2026 (MATD3 in OpenSim, doi 10.1007/s11517-026-03634-9).

HILO with walking speed as the objective: Song & Collins 2021; multi-objective speed and economy in older adults, who also needed longer to adapt (Lakmazaheri et al., JNER 2024, doi 10.1186/s12984-023-01287-5); Kim & Sergi 2026. Hip HILO beyond level walking: stair climbing, where metabolic rate converged after about 18 iterations but most parameters had not converged within 20 (Park et al., IEEE TBME 2025, doi 10.1109/TBME.2025.3536516).

Fast, real-world and user-driven HILO: outdoor ankle optimisation (Slade et al., Nature 2022, doi 10.1038/s41586-022-05191-1); a portable hip-extension exosuit, from the sprint-exosuit lab, optimised outdoors in 3 min 24 s (Nam et al., Adv. Robot. Res. 2026, online 2025, doi 10.1002/adrr.202400027); preference-based hip-exoskeleton self-tuning in about 11 min (Schäfer et al., npj Biomed. Innov. 2026, doi 10.1038/s44385-026-00085-7).

Training design and feedback change how fast people adapt: Poggensee & Collins 2021; biofeedback (Lakmazaheri & Collins, IEEE TNSRE 2026, doi 10.1109/TNSRE.2025.3650042); adaptive-gain myoelectric control (Koller et al., JNER 2015, doi 10.1186/s12984-015-0086-5).
open_gaps: Which equilibrium does SMAT reach? At matched budgets, train fast-device/slow-human, slow-device/fast-human and simultaneous schedules, then cross-play every final human checkpoint against every device checkpoint. Test whether outcomes shift as leader-follower theory predicts, checking the pipeline first on a toy quadratic game (Chasnov-style).

A rate-limited simulated human: cap per-stage human policy change (KL or step budget) to mimic published adaptation timescales, then test whether a device policy trained against it transfers better to held-out human policies than one trained against a freely learning PPO human. The calibration to real minutes stays indirect and must be stated as such.

Simulated sprint HILO under realistic budgets: extend the Kutulakos & Slade bench to a sprint-time surrogate from the musculoskeletal sprinter, with 10-20 fatigue-limited evaluations per session, a novice-drift scenario, and BO, dynamic BO and CMA-ES compared. The output is the optimiser a later human study should pre-register.

Objective mismatch in simulation: in the same simulated sprinter, compare assistance optimised for 200 m time with assistance optimised for muscle activation or a metabolic proxy, and quantify the differences in timing and magnitude before any human work. This is the sprint version of the Song & Collins 2021 question.

Tabular falsification of the CaMDP conditions: discretise a reduced human-exoskeleton task, check the information and dominance conditions directly, and run alternation, instantaneous-threshold and accumulated-threshold schedules against the PPO results (following KB reading-06).
unverifiable: No seed was unverifiable: all 13 named seeds resolved to arXiv, Crossref or bioRxiv records whose titles matched (2026-09-23). The notes below are verification notes, not failures.

It compares BO with gradient descent on step frequency in unaided walking, not hip-exosuit parameters. Verified but not selected; Ding 2018 covers hip HILO.
